Neonatal Pearly-eyed thrashers emerge from eggs incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] with a remarkably modest body mass of just 5 grams [Wwb = 5 grams], reflecting the altricial developmental strategy common among Mimidae. This initial wet weight is among the lowest recorded for passerines of comparable adult size, suggesting that the species channels energy into rapid post-hatching growth rather than into yolk reserves. The incubation period that precedes hatching is approximately 14 days [ab = approximately 14 days], a value derived from work on the curve-billed thrasher Toxostoma curvirostre, which exhibits a similar nest architecture and at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]thermal regime. Nestlings are brooded continuously during the first week, with parents maintaining a near-constant temperature within the nest cup, a behavior that buffers the altricial chicks from diurnal temperature fluctuations. By the time they reach the fledgling stage, these birds have undergone a rapid transformation in mass and feather development, transitioning from a 5 gram neonate to a substantially heavier juvenile capable of short flights.

As the nestling period progresses, young thrashers achieve a crucial developmental milestone under the species' typical active metabolic temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Fledging, defined as the first sustained flight and departure from the nest, occurs at 10 days after hatching [tx = 10 days after hatching], a value that aligns closely with data reported for the brown thrasher Toxostoma rufum at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This brief nestling phase is characteristic of species that face high predation pressure on ground-level nests; a rapid exit reduces the window of vulnerability. During these ten days, parental provisioning is intense, with both adults delivering insects, fruits, and small reptiles to the rapidly growing brood. The fledglings remain dependent on their parents for an additional period after nest departure, but the achievement of flight at this early age marks a significant transition in their life history. Partial wing feathers develop quickly in the confined nest space, enabling this precocial departure from the nest structure itself.

The trajectory toward sexual maturity unfolds over a longer timescale, beginning with puberty, which is estimated at 30 days after hatching [tp = 30 days after hatching] when body temperatures are maintained at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This value, also drawn from studies of Toxostoma rufum, suggests that gonadal maturation in the Pearly-eyed thrasher is remarkably rapid for a tropical passerine, likely driven by the consistent thermal environment that supports accelerated physiological development. Juveniles attaining this milestone show the first signs of gonadal recrudescence, although they do not immediately engage in breeding activities. Instead, a substantial delay occurs before the initiation of the first reproductive attempt. First brood production is not observed until 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching] under the same thermal conditions of 41.6 °C, indicating that while sexual maturation occurs early in life, the expression of full reproductive behavior is deferred by nearly a full year at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This lag likely reflects the time required for territory acquisition and pair bonding in a species that nests in tree cavities or palm fronds.

Reproductive output in this species is modest but sustained across the adult lifespan. Under favorable thermal conditions near 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], Pearly-eyed thrashers typically lay 2 to 4 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 to 4 eggs per clutch], with females capable of producing approximately 0.6 to 1.2 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 0.6 to 1.2 clutches per year], a pattern that trades off against extended parental care and a relatively long adult lifespan. Such reproductive traits are consistent with a tropical island endemic that faces resource limitations and reduced seasonality compared to temperate relatives. The species also exhibits plasticity in clutch size: first-year breeders tend toward the lower end of the range with 2 eggs, while experienced adults in high-quality habitats may consistently produce 4 eggs per clutch. Nest success rates in natural cavities further modulate the effective number of fledglings produced annually.

Lifespan in the Pearly-eyed thrasher is considerable for a passerine of its size, with the oldest documented individuals reaching 17 years [am = 17 years] when core body temperatures are maintained at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This longevity is notable among tropical mímids, many of which rarely exceed a decade in the wild. The ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown adults is approximately 100.48 grams [Wwi = approximately 100.48 grams], making this one of the larger members of the family Mimidae in the Caribbean region. This body mass is achieved through a growth trajectory that plateaus during the first year, after which birds enter a prolonged adult phase characterized by stable mass and sustained reproductive output. The combination of a moderate lifespan, modest annual fecundity, and substantial adult body mass aligns with a slow-paced life history strategy typical of island endemics that face fewer seasonal resource pulses but also encounter higher stochastic mortality from hurricanes and introduced predators.
